blocks.text: Go deep before you go wide. DFS is the foundation behind cycle detection, pathfinding, topological sort, and connected components.
DFS in action going deep along path 1 → 2 → 4 before backtracking to explore 5, 3, 6, 7
In the previous article we learned what a graph is vertices, edges, directed vs undirected, adjacency lists and matrices. Now it's time to actually move through a graph.
Depth-First Search (DFS) is one of the two fundamental graph traversal algorithms. The idea is simple: go as deep as possible before backtracking.
DFS powers cycle detection, topological sort, connected components, pathfinding, and much more.
DFS explores a graph by starting at a source node and diving as far as possible along each branch before backing up and trying the next one.
It follows the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle naturally implemented using recursion (the call stack) or an explicit stack.
KEY INTUITION: Think of DFS like exploring a maze. Pick a corridor and keep walking until you hit a dead end. Then backtrack to the last junction and try a different path.

items:
Start at a node
Mark it as visited and process it.

Backtrack
When all neighbours are visited, return to the previous node.

Handle disconnected graphs
Start DFS again from any unvisited node until all nodes are covered.

Time and Space Complexity
DFS visits every vertex and every edge exactly once.

NOTE: In the worst case (a path graph), the recursion depth equals V. For very deep graphs, prefer the iterative version to avoid a stack overflow.

Before diving into DFS problems, understand these terms they appear in almost every DFS interview question.

• Visited array A boolean array of size V. Tracks which nodes DFS has already processed. Without it, DFS loops forever on cycles.
  • Back edge An edge pointing to an ancestor in the DFS tree. Finding a back edge means the graph has a cycle.
  • Tree edge An edge used by DFS to discover a new node. These form the DFS tree.
  • DFS tree The spanning tree built from tree edges during traversal. Used in algorithms like Tarjan's and Kosaraju's.
  • Discovery / Finish time The step when DFS first visits a node (discovery) and when it finishes processing all its neighbours (finish). Used in topological sort.
  • Connected component A maximal set of nodes reachable from each other. Each separate DFS call from dfsAll finds one new component.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406028611-316886962.png

• Cycle detection Detect back edges in directed or undirected graphs. Used to validate DAGs.
  • Topological sort Order tasks with dependencies. DFS finish-time ordering gives the correct order.
  • Connected components Count separate islands/components in a graph. Each DFS from an unvisited node finds one component.
  • Maze / puzzle solving Explore all possible paths and backtrack. DFS naturally explores every route.
  • SCC (Tarjan / Kosaraju) Find strongly connected components in directed graphs using DFS-based algorithms.
  • Bridge / articulation point Identify critical edges or vertices whose removal disconnects the graph.
